content.value_statement: Logseq database queries can be hard to write and debug. This skill gives structured Datalog guidance, examples, and optimization advice for graph data work.
actual_capabilities: Explains Logseq Datalog query structure, including find, input, and where clauses.
Provides patterns for tags, properties, tasks, journals, and classes.
Shows pull syntax for selected attributes, nested references, and reverse references.
Guides aggregation, negation, or clauses, and reusable rule patterns.
Suggests performance improvements for selective clauses and attribute selection.
Translates simple Logseq query ideas into full Datalog query shapes.
limitations: It does not connect to a live Logseq graph or inspect private notes.
It cannot guarantee query results without the user graph schema and sample data.
It focuses on Logseq database graphs, not Markdown graph queries.
Advanced query blocks may still need testing inside Logseq.

use_cases.title: Create a Reading Query
use_cases.description: Build a query that finds books, authors, ratings, or missing metadata in a Logseq graph.

use_cases.title: Improve Task Dashboards
use_cases.description: Design task queries that filter by status, deadline, priority, and project tags.

use_cases.title: Debug Plugin Queries
use_cases.description: Shape Datascript queries for plugin code and parameterized Logseq database calls.

prompt_templates.title: Find Basic Blocks
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me write a Logseq Datalog query that finds blocks with a specific tag and returns their titles.

prompt_templates.title: Filter by Properties
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Logseq Datalog query for tasks with a status, deadline range, and priority value. Explain each clause.

prompt_templates.title: Use Pull and Rules
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a Logseq query that uses pull syntax and reusable rules for related blocks. Include performance notes.

prompt_templates.title: Optimize a Query Block
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Logseq query concept for performance, attribute selection, and result shaping before I test it.

output_examples.input: Find all books without a rating property.
output_examples.output: The skill explains a negation pattern, identifies the book tag filter, and returns a query plan for missing ratings.

output_examples.input: Show overdue tasks with high priority.
output_examples.output: The skill suggests deadline and priority filters, notes required inputs, and explains how to bind today as a parameter.
The skill recommends selective clauses first, fewer pulled attributes, and limits for large nested results.

best_practices: Provide the relevant Logseq graph type, property names, and expected result shape.
Ask for selected attributes instead of full entity pulls when performance matters.
Test generated query blocks in Logseq with a small result set first.
anti_patterns: Do not request broad wildcard pulls when only a few attributes are needed.
Do not mix Markdown graph attributes with database graph attributes without checking schema differences.
Do not assume property names are standard across different Logseq graphs.

faq.question: Does this skill access my Logseq graph?
faq.answer: No. It provides query guidance and examples, but it does not read your local graph data.

faq.question: Can it write plugin database queries?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes Datascript query patterns that can guide Logseq plugin database calls.

faq.question: Does it support Markdown graphs?
faq.answer: It is focused on Logseq database graphs. Markdown graph attributes may need different query patterns.

faq.question: Can it optimize slow queries?
faq.answer: It can suggest clause ordering, selective attributes, and smaller pulls. Real performance depends on your graph data.

faq.question: Can it explain existing Datalog?
faq.answer: Yes. Provide the query and expected result, and it can explain clauses, variables, and likely issues.

faq.question: Is coding experience required?
faq.answer: Basic Logseq knowledge is enough for simple prompts. Advanced query blocks benefit from Datalog familiarity.
